pharm: A long-acting, pegylated erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (continuous erythropoietin receptor activator, CERA) that stimulates erythropoiesis to treat anemia of chronic kidney disease, dosed as infrequently as once monthly because of its prolonged half-life. Marketed as Mircera.
quick: ESA-naive: 0.6 mcg/kg every 2 weeks IV/SC; non-dialysis option 1.2 mcg/kg monthly SC
Not applicable - injectable; no food interaction
Limited human data; animal bone malformations at high doses; use only if needed
Endogenous erythropoietin is in human milk; likely compatible, limited data
Indication is anemia of CKD itself; titrate to hemoglobin, not by CrCl
Hemoglobin, blood pressure, iron status, signs of thrombosis/PRCA
summary: Methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta (Mircera) is a long-acting erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (a continuous erythropoietin receptor activator) indicated for the treatment of anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in adults (on and not on dialysis) and in pediatric patients 3 months to 17 years converting from another ESA after hemoglobin has stabilized. Because of its long half-life (about 5 days) it can be given every 2 weeks or once monthly by IV or subcutaneous injection. It carries a boxed warning: ESAs increase the risk of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism, vascular access thrombosis, and tumor progression. Use the lowest dose to avoid red blood cell transfusions, target hemoglobin should not exceed about 11 g/dL, and it is not indicated for chemotherapy-induced anemia.
indications: Treatment of anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in adults on dialysis and not on dialysis
Treatment of anemia associated with CKD in pediatric patients 3 months to 17 years of age who are converting from another ESA after hemoglobin was stabilized

dosage.n: Titrate to lowest dose maintaining hemoglobin and avoiding transfusion

admin: Administer by intravenous or subcutaneous injection; use the IV route in hemodialysis patients when feasible
Use the prefilled syringe as a single dose; it is preservative-free - discard any unused portion
Do not shake the syringe vigorously; allow refrigerated product to reach room temperature before injecting if desired
Ensure adequate iron stores (transferrin saturation and ferritin) before and during therapy
Control blood pressure before starting and during therapy; do not start if hypertension is uncontrolled
Use the lowest dose sufficient to reduce the need for red blood cell transfusions
moa: Methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta is a continuous erythropoietin receptor activator (CERA). Like endogenous erythropoietin it binds to and activates the erythropoietin receptor on erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, stimulating their proliferation and differentiation into mature red blood cells. Its pegylated structure gives it a different interaction with the receptor and a markedly prolonged half-life compared with epoetin, allowing extended (every 2-week or monthly) dosing intervals. Adequate iron is required for an effective erythropoietic response.

absolute: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) that begins after treatment with Mircera or other erythropoietin protein drugs
Serious or severe allergic reactions to methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta (e.g., anaphylaxis, angioedema, bronchospasm, urticaria)
relative: Active malignancy (ESAs may shorten survival/promote tumor progression)
History of stroke, thromboembolism, or cardiovascular disease
Iron deficiency or other causes of hyporesponsiveness
monitor: Hemoglobin (do not exceed the target; rapid rises increase risk)
Signs of thrombosis (vascular access, DVT/PE, MI, stroke) and new/loss of response suggesting PRCA

preg: There are limited human data. Animal studies showed adverse developmental effects, including bone malformations, at doses about 17 or more times the recommended human dose. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus; treat anemia to avoid maternal transfusion as clinically indicated.
lact: There are no data on the presence of methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta in human milk; endogenous erythropoietin is present in human milk. Because it is a large protein likely degraded in the infant's gastrointestinal tract, significant absorption by the breastfed infant is unlikely; breastfeeding is generally considered compatible. Consider the mother's clinical need and the benefits of breastfeeding.
renal: The drug treats anemia caused by chronic kidney disease, so renal impairment is the indication rather than a contraindication. Dosing is titrated to hemoglobin response, not to creatinine clearance. Use the lowest dose that reduces the need for transfusion and avoid hemoglobin above approximately 11 g/dL (dialysis) / target ranges per label.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment for hepatic impairment is defined in the labeling; clinical experience in significant hepatic impairment is limited, so use with appropriate monitoring.

moderate: Iron deficiency / inadequate iron supplementation - blunts the erythropoietic response (functional interaction)
minor: No formal cytochrome P450-mediated drug interactions described
interactions.diagnostics: Raises hematocrit/hemoglobin and reticulocyte count; can increase blood pressure readings.

serious: Increased mortality and cardiovascular events (MI, stroke)
Tumor progression or recurrence in patients with cancer
rare: Serious allergic reactions including anaphylaxis and angioedema
Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN reported with ESAs)

monitoring: Hemoglobin (initially weekly to biweekly, then per stability; keep within target, avoid >11 g/dL excursions and rapid rises)
Blood pressure at baseline and during therapy
Iron status - ferritin and transferrin saturation
Signs and symptoms of thromboembolism and cardiovascular events
Loss of hemoglobin response / sudden drop suggesting pure red cell aplasia
counsel: This medicine treats anemia caused by kidney disease by helping your body make red blood cells; it is given by injection every 2 weeks or once a month
Keep all appointments for blood tests - your dose is adjusted based on your hemoglobin level
Tell your doctor right away about chest pain, trouble breathing, sudden weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, or pain/swelling in a leg (signs of clots or stroke)
Report severe headache, blurred vision, or very high blood pressure readings
Take iron or other supplements exactly as prescribed - the medicine needs iron to work
Store in the refrigerator and protect from light; do not shake the syringe
pk: Hemoglobin increase typically seen 7-15 days after the first dose
Long-acting: terminal half-life ~119 hours IV / ~124 hours SC (~5 days)
Refrigerate 2-8 C; protect from light; do not freeze or shake
pearls: BOXED WARNING (class effect for ESAs): increased death, MI, stroke, thromboembolism, vascular-access thrombosis, and tumor progression
Long-acting CERA - dosing every 2 weeks or once monthly, unlike short-acting epoetin
Use the lowest dose to avoid transfusion; do not chase a normal hemoglobin - keep within target (avoid >11 g/dL)
NOT indicated for chemotherapy-induced anemia (a dose-ranging trial was stopped early for increased mortality)
Ensure adequate iron and control blood pressure before and during therapy
Sudden loss of response with a low reticulocyte count suggests antibody-mediated pure red cell aplasia - stop the drug and evaluate
missed: This medicine is given by a healthcare provider on a fixed schedule. If a scheduled dose is missed, administer it as soon as possible and resume the regular every-2-week or monthly schedule; do not give two doses close together. Contact the clinic to reschedule.
overdose: Overdose can cause an excessive rise in hemoglobin/hematocrit with increased risk of hypertension, headache, seizures, and thromboembolic events (including stroke and myocardial infarction). Management is to withhold further doses, monitor hemoglobin and blood pressure, treat hypertension and complications supportively, and perform phlebotomy if polycythemia is clinically significant.
